entry: Cell or organism with one or more whip-like appendages called [[Flagellum|flagella]]. The term describes a cell construction found in many prokaryotes and eukaryotes, and it does not imply a specific relationship among the organisms that bear flagella. Flagella are generally used for propulsion and sometimes to create currents that bring in food. In some flagellates they direct food into a cytostome, or mouth. Flagellates form a polyphyletic group of over 8,000 described species, many of them single-celled [[Protist|protists]]. Many parasites are flagellates in at least one life-cycle stage, including Naegleria, Trichomonas and Plasmodium. In aquatic ecosystems, flagellates are major consumers of bacteria and other protists.

Hair-like cellular appendage that provides motility. Flagella protrude from certain plant and animal sperm cells, from [[Spore|fungal spores]] (zoospores) and from many [[Microorganism|microorganisms]]. The name is [[Latin]] for "whip" or "scourge," describing the lash-like swimming motion. Structure, protein composition and propulsion differ among the [[Bacteria]], [[Archaea]] and Eukaryota domains, but all provide motility. Bacterial flagella are helical filaments turned by rotary motors at their base; the archaeal version, the archaellum, is superficially similar but considered non-homologous. Eukaryotic flagella are membrane projections supported by the cytoskeleton that bend back and forth, with nine doublet microtubules surrounding two central singlets. A cell may have zero, one or many flagella. *Helicobacter pylori* uses its flagella to swim through the stomach to the mucous lining, and *Salmonella typhimurium* can sense wetness with them.

Art form of song, guitar and dance from southern Spain. It developed within the *gitano* ([[Romani people|Romani]]) subculture of [[Andalusia]] and has also been present in Extremadura and Murcia. Its forms combine song, guitar, dance, *compás*, modal and tonal harmony, *falsetas*, handclaps and footwork. The identity of a *palo*, or musical form, depends on rhythmic cycle, mode, chord progression, stanzaic form and geographic origin. The oldest record dates to 1774, in José Cadalso's *Las Cartas Marruecas*. The term first referred to the music genre in an 1847 newspaper article, after it had long designated the Romani people themselves. On 16 November 2010, [[UNESCO]] declared flamenco one of the Masterpieces of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.

Wading bird of the family Phoenicopteridae, the only living family in the order Phoenicopteriformes. Six living species occur in tropical and subtropical regions: four in the Americas, including the Caribbean, and two in Afro-Eurasia. Their pink plumage results from [[Carotenoid|carotenoids]] in their diet. Flamingos have long legs, sinuous necks and downward-curving bills, and they feed by sweeping their heads through water and filtering algae, crustaceans and small invertebrates with lamellae in their bills. They are highly gregarious, forming colonies called flamboyances that may hold hundreds of thousands of birds. Breeding pairs build conical mud nests, and the female lays a single egg. The lesser flamingo is the smallest species and often forms flocks of up to a million birds.

Dutch-speaking northern region of [[Belgium]]. Most Flemings live in the Flemish Region, a federal state with its own elected government. Its official capital is the [[City of Brussels]], which lies outside that region in the Brussels-Capital Region. Mainly flat, Flanders includes the whole Belgian coast on the North Sea. As of January 2024, 6,821,770 people, or 58%, of Belgium's inhabitants lived there, at a density of 501/km². Its five provinces are Antwerp, East Flanders, Flemish Brabant, Limburg and West Flanders. The original County of Flanders, around AD 900, grew into one of the richest and most urbanized parts of Europe, with [[Ghent]], [[Bruges]] and [[Antwerp]] trading and weaving wool. Industrialization occurred mainly in French-speaking [[Wallonia]], but in the late 20th century Flanders' economy modernized rapidly, and it is now among the wealthiest regions in Europe. The official language is [[Dutch language|Dutch]].

Rapid flooding of low-lying areas such as washes, rivers and dry lakes. They may follow heavy rain from severe [[Thunderstorm|thunderstorms]], hurricanes or tropical storms, or meltwater from ice and snow, and are distinguished from regular floods by fewer than six hours between rainfall and flooding. The collapse of a natural ice or debris dam, or of a man-made dam, can also trigger them. In the United States they cause more deaths in an average year than lightning, tornadoes or hurricanes. More than half of their fatalities involve people swept away in vehicles.

Archaic, scientifically disproven conception of Earth as a plane or disk. Many ancient societies held a flat-Earth cosmography. The idea of a spherical Earth appeared with [[Pythagoras]] in the 6th century BC, and by about 330 BC [[Aristotle]] had provided strong empirical evidence for a sphere. The belief that medieval Europeans generally thought Earth was flat is a historical myth, created in the 17th century by Protestants. Since the 2010s, social media has spread flat-Earth conspiracy theories, yet firm belief in a flat Earth stays below 2% in every age group.

Electronic display of text or images, much thinner than cathode-ray tubes. Usually less than 10 centimeters thick, flat-panel displays are lightweight and offer better linearity, higher resolution and contrast than typical consumer televisions of earlier eras. By 2016 they had almost completely replaced CRT displays. Most use [[Liquid-crystal display|LCD]] or [[Light-emitting diode|LED]] technologies, sometimes combined, and smartphones often use [[OLED]] panels. Volatile displays, such as LCDs, must be refreshed to keep their state and show an image only when powered; static displays, such as e-ink, retain content without power. The first engineering proposal for a flat-panel television came from [[General Electric]] in 1954. The first production flat-panel display, the Aiken tube, was made in limited numbers in 1958 and used by the military before conventional technologies overtook it.

Ray-finned fishes that rest on one side of the seafloor. In adults both eyes lie on the upper side of the head, because one eye migrates across the skull during juvenile metamorphosis, a unique asymmetry among vertebrates. The upper surface is often pigmented for [[Camouflage|camouflage]], while the blind side is pale. Some families have eyes usually on the right side of the body, others on the left. Flatfishes live in oceans worldwide, with most species between 0 and 500 m deep and species diversity centered in the Indo-West Pacific. Many enter brackish or fresh water. The tonguefish *Symphurus thermophilus* congregates around sulfur at [[Hydrothermal vent|hydrothermal vents]]. Many species are important to fisheries, including halibut, flounder, sole and turbot.

Triangular 22-story steel-framed skyscraper in [[Manhattan]], New York City. Designed by Daniel Burnham and Frederick P. Dinkelberg, it opened on October 1, 1902, as headquarters of the Fuller Company and was originally named the Fuller Building. Its name derives from its shape, which recalls a cast-iron clothes iron. The facade has a [[Limestone|limestone]] base and glazed terracotta upper stories. Designated a New York City landmark in 1966 and a National Historic Landmark in 1989, it was converted to residential condominiums, a project completed in 2026.

Expulsion of gas from the intestines through the [[Anus|anus]]. Flatus, the medical term for intestinal gas, is generated in the stomach or bowels, partly from swallowed air. Passing it is normal, though volume and frequency vary greatly. Intestinal gas is mostly odorless, consisting mainly of nitrogen, carbon dioxide and hydrogen, with [[Methane]] in some people. Odor comes from sulfur compounds in less than 1% of its volume. Excessive flatus may signal [[Irritable bowel syndrome|irritable bowel syndrome]], celiac disease or lactose intolerance. Many societies regard it as taboo.

Soft-bodied, unsegmented bilaterian invertebrate of the phylum Platyhelminthes. Lacking a body cavity and circulatory and respiratory organs, flatworms rely on flattened shapes that let oxygen and nutrients diffuse through the body. Their single digestive opening serves for both intake and waste removal, so food cannot be processed continuously. Most free-living species are predators in water or humid terrestrial habitats. The parasitic [[Cestoda|tapeworms]] and flukes have complex life cycles, while monogeneans are external parasites of aquatic animals. Since the mid-1980s, analyses have placed the Acoelomorpha as basal bilaterians, and over 20,000 species are known. A planarian introduced to control the giant African [[Snail|snail]] in the Philippines and the Maldives now threatens native snails and should not be used for biological control. New Zealand planarians prey on [[Earthworm|earthworms]] in northwestern Europe.

Roman general and statesman of the closing period of the [[Western Roman Empire]]. As the most influential man in the Empire from 433 to 454, he managed policy toward barbarian federate groups settled in the West. In 451 he mustered a large Roman and allied army that defeated [[Attila]] at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains, ending Attila's invasion of Gaul. Attila's forces invaded Italy the following year, an incursion remembered for the Sack of Aquileia and the intercession of [[Pope Leo I]]. In 454, Aetius was assassinated by Emperor Valentinian III. Historians often call him the "Last of the Romans." As a youth he lived at the courts of Visigothic and Hunnic rulers, which some historians credit with giving him martial vigor.

Annual flowering plant, *Linum usitatissimum*, grown for fiber and seed. Native from the eastern Mediterranean to India, it was first domesticated in the [[Fertile Crescent]] and is cultivated in temperate climates. Textiles made from its fibers are known as [[Linen]], traditionally used for bed sheets and table linen. Its seeds yield flaxseed or linseed and linseed oil. Wild flax fibers from Dzudzuana Cave in present-day Georgia date to 30,000 years ago, and domesticated flax appeared around 9,000 years ago. Flax was extensively cultivated in [[Ancient Egypt]], where mummies were embalmed with linen. [[Carl Linnaeus]] coined the scientific name in 1753. Cultivated plants grow to 1.2 meters tall and need little fertilizer or pesticide.

Wingless insect of the order Siphonaptera, an external parasite of mammals and birds. About 2,500 species feed on the blood of their hosts. Adults are 1.5 to 3.3 millimeters long, with laterally compressed bodies that move through fur or feathers and hind legs adapted for jumping. A flea can jump up to 18 centimeters vertically and 33 centimeters horizontally, second only to the froghopper among animals relative to body size. Each species usually specializes on one host species. The earliest known fleas lived in the Middle Jurassic. The oriental rat flea, *Xenopsylla cheopis*, transmits [[Yersinia pestis]], which causes bubonic plague; outbreaks included the Plague of Justinian, about 540, and the [[Black Death]], about 1350.

British and American rock band. Formed in London in 1967, it began as a British blues band, and its instrumental "Albatross" reached No. 1 in the UK in 1968. After recruiting [[Stevie Nicks]] and Lindsey Buckingham in 1974, the band released *Fleetwood Mac* (1975), which topped the Billboard 200. *Rumours* (1977) is among the best-selling albums of all time and won the Grammy Award for Album of the Year. The band has sold more than 120 million records. Buckingham was fired in 2018.

Stylized lily used as a [[Heraldry|heraldic]] charge. It appeared on the coat of arms of France from the High Middle Ages until the French Revolution in 1789, and it still appears in the arms of Spain, Quebec and Canada as a sign of France's royal dynasty. The lily symbolized purity and, in Christianity, the Immaculate Conception. An 18th-century French naturalist argued that the design derives from the [[Iris (plant)|iris]], which grows along the Lys river in Flanders. The name derives from Latin *lilium* and French *lis*.

Motion of an object through air or space without contact with a planetary surface. Flight may be achieved through aerodynamic lift, propulsive thrust, buoyancy or ballistic movement. Among living things, powered flight has evolved in birds, bats and [[Insect|insects]], and insects were the first animals to fly. Bats are the only mammals capable of sustained level flight, and gliding evolved in many other groups. [[Pterosaur|Pterosaurs]], reptiles contemporary with the dinosaurs, were also powerful fliers. Human flight includes airplanes, helicopters, airships and balloons, and rockets may propel spacecraft. [[Aerospace engineering|Aerospace engineering]] has three subfields: aeronautics, astronautics and ballistics. The Wright brothers achieved the first powered, controlled flight in 1903.

Electronic recording device placed in an aircraft to aid investigation of accidents. Colloquially called a "black box," it is painted bright orange for recovery. The flight data recorder logs dozens of parameters several times per second, while the cockpit voice recorder preserves cockpit sound; the two may be combined. Required to survive an impact of 3,400 g and temperatures above 1,000 °C, recorders have been mandatory on U.S. commercial aircraft since 1967. After [[Malaysia Airlines Flight 370]] disappeared in 2014, commentators called for live data streaming to the ground.

Sedimentary, cryptocrystalline form of the mineral [[Quartz|quartz]]. A variety of [[Chert|chert]] found mainly as nodules in chalk and limestone, flint is usually dark gray or black inside, with a glassy or waxy look and a rough, white outer layer. When broken it forms sharp edges used for knives and scrapers, and flint tools date back more than three million years. It is one of the primary materials that define the [[Stone Age]]. Flint Ridge in Ohio supplied material traded across the eastern United States. Struck against steel, flint produces sparks that ignite tinder or the gunpowder of a flintlock.

Methods for reducing or preventing the harmful effects of floodwaters. Structural flood control uses physical solutions such as [[Reservoir|reservoirs]], [[Levee|levees]], dredging and diversions. Non-structural methods include land-use planning, advanced warning systems, flood insurance and [[Zoning]] ordinances. Flood mitigation is a broader concept that includes prevention, prediction and proofing, while flood risk management focuses on reducing risk through assessment. Because [[Climate change|climate change]] has increased flood risk and intensity, management is part of climate adaptation. Best practice favors soft infrastructure such as marshes and floodplains, and flooding is studied at three levels: individual properties, small communities and whole towns or cities.

Land beside a [[River|river]] flooded during periods of high discharge. It extends from the river channel banks to the base of the enclosing valley. Its soils of clays, silts, sands and gravels are deposited by floods, giving it high fertility that supports farming in regions such as the [[Nile]] and Mississippi basins. Most floodplains form through deposition on the inside of [[Meander|meanders]], where point bars build up, and by overbank flow that deposits sediment on natural levees and in wetlands. In undisturbed systems, overbank flow occurs about every one to two years. Avulsion, when a river abandons its channel belt for a new one, occurs at intervals of 10 to 1000 years.

Bottom surface of an enclosed space such as a [[Room|room]] or [[Vehicle|vehicle]]. Floors range from simple dirt in a [[Cave|cave]] to layered surfaces made with modern technology, and may be stone, wood, bamboo, metal or any other load-bearing material. A typical floor has a subfloor for support and a floor covering for walking; in modern buildings the subfloor often holds wiring and plumbing. Floors rest on beams, joists or prefabricated hollow-core slabs. Building levels are often called floors, though American English sometimes uses storeys or stories. Special floor structures include floating floors for noise reduction, [[Glass]] floors in elevators, raised floors for accessible utilities, sprung floors for athletes and raked floors for stage views.

Removable storage medium of a thin, flexible magnetic disk in a plastic shell. IBM introduced the first floppy disks in 1971, with an 8-inch diameter. The 5¼-inch and then 3½-inch formats followed, and by the mid-1990s the 3½-inch disk, with higher capacity and a rigid case, had become dominant. Many programs still use save icons that depict floppy disks. The format has been superseded by [[USB]] flash drives, memory cards, [[Optical disc|optical discs]] and cloud storage, though some legacy industrial equipment still uses floppy drives.

Mother church of the Catholic Archdiocese of Florence, Italy, formally the Cathedral of Saint Mary of the Flower. Begun in 1296 in the [[Gothic architecture|Gothic]] style to a design by Arnolfo di Cambio, it was completed by 1436 with a dome engineered by [[Filippo Brunelleschi]]. Its exterior is faced with polychrome marble panels in green, pink and white, and the 19th-century Gothic Revival western façade is by Emilio De Fabris. The cathedral complex in the Piazza del Duomo includes the Florence Baptistery and [[Giotto]]'s Campanile, and the three buildings form part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The dome is still the largest masonry dome ever constructed.
